source: Klein, Calderwood & Clinton-Cirocco (1986/1988) Rapid decision making on the fireground (US Army Research Institute report)
finding: Founding RPD study. Interviews with experienced fireground commanders found that most hard decisions were made by recognizing a situation as typical and acting on the first workable option. Comparing several options side by side was rare. Seen only in a search-result excerpt; the PDF was blocked (HTTP 403).
numbers: As quoted in the excerpt: 26 commanders (mean 23 years experience), 156 probed decision points, evidence of concurrent comparison of 2+ options in under 12%, over 80% single recognized prototype.
quote: In less than 12% of them was there any evidence of simultaneous comparisons and relative evaluation of two or more options.
limits: Retrospective interviews, no control group, no outcome check against a counterfactual. Self-report of what the commander did. Dates in sources vary (1985, 1986, 1988). Not read in full.
agent_relevance: The base claim behind S0 quick mode: with a strong pattern match, generate one option and test it, do not enumerate. Note it says nothing about whether the first option was right.

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: From Theory to Toolbox, Frontiers in Psychology 7:54
finding: Klein's own history of NDM. States the RPD model accounted for 80-90% of firefighter decisions and lists replications by other teams: military leaders (Schmitt & Klein 1999), firefighters (Keren et al. 2013), offshore oil platform managers (Skriver 1998). Says RPD was tested and supported by Klein et al. 1995 and Johnson & Raab 2003.
numbers: RPD accounted for 80-90% of firefighter decisions. RPD depended on 10-20 years of experience. 12 NDM conferences held by 2016. 16 commentaries answered Lipshitz et al. 2001.
quote: The RPD model accounted for 80-90% of the decisions that firefighters made.
limits: Written by the model's author. The listed replications are field interviews by the same research tradition, not blind or lab replications. The 80-90% range is wider and higher than the 80% in the original report.
agent_relevance: The honest summary of support: repeated across domains by interview methods, but no independent test of whether recognition decisions beat analysis.

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: From Theory to Toolbox, section on what NDM no longer claims
finding: Klein's list of revised beliefs. Experienced people can handle time pressure by pattern matching and never compare options. Insights arise by detecting contradictions and anomalies, not only by overcoming mental sets. Gathering more information does not always reduce uncertainty.
numbers: No figures. Claims: 'performance seems to go down when too much information is gathered'.
quote: experienced decision-makers can draw on patterns to handle time pressure and never even compare options
limits: Position statement, not data. Uncertainty-from-framing claim is asserted, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and the idea that more sampling or more information is not the default fix. Doubt should come from a signal of mismatch, not from a schedule.

source: Lipshitz, Klein, Orasanu & Salas (2001) Taking stock of naturalistic decision making, J Behav Decis Making; 16 commentaries
finding: Lead article that drew 16 commentaries. Lab decision researchers said NDM needed more rigorous, controlled methods and clearer testable claims. Known only second-hand through Klein & Wright 2016, which describes the criticism and calls it misguided.
numbers: 16 commentaries (from Klein & Wright 2016). No effect sizes.
limits: Original not opened. The critique is about method, so it cannot be scored as a failed replication.
agent_relevance: Reminds us that RPD has few controlled tests. Any S0 rule drawn from it is single-source until tested on our own tasks.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree, American Psychologist 64(6):515-526
finding: Joint paper by the rival camps (heuristics-and-biases vs NDM). They agree that intuitive judgment is trustworthy only when the environment has stable cues that can be learned, and the person had prolonged practice with good feedback. Full text could not be opened (APA and PubMed pages blocked); condition summary comes from search-result commentary.
numbers: No sample. Two stated conditions: (1) regular, predictable environment; (2) prolonged practice with honest feedback.
limits: Not read this session. Confidence is not a guide to validity under these conditions. Kahneman later said they disagreed often despite the subtitle.
agent_relevance: Gives the gate for S0: allow a fast single answer only on task types where our own measured history shows regularity and clean feedback; otherwise route to checks (G2, G3).

source: Johnson & Raab (2003) Take the first: option-generation and resulting choices, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 91(2):215-229
finding: Handball players shown game video clips generated options. The first options generated were better than later ones, and choosing the first beat choosing after longer deliberation. Supports take-the-first as a search rule inside RPD. Only the title and a secondary description were seen.
numbers: Exact N and effect sizes not read.
limits: Sport clips, expert raters judged quality. One sport. Not read.
agent_relevance: A direct test that first option beats later options for experts in a domain with learned cues. Suggests ordering candidates by prior validity and stopping early when a check passes.

source: Raab & Gigerenzer (2015) The power of simplicity: a fast-and-frugal heuristics approach to performance science, Frontiers in Psychology 6:1672
finding: Reviews take-the-first. Evidence in team handball (Johnson & Raab 2003) and basketball (Hepler & Feltz 2011). Tendency to take the first option is changed by situation, emotion and personality. Learned over years of expertise (Raab & Johnson 2007 longitudinal). Transferred to nursing, navigation, law, medicine, consumer choice, engineering.
numbers: No new data. Fast-and-frugal tree example: Michigan hospital sent about 90% of chest-pain patients to coronary care when only about 25% had a coronary problem (Green & Mehr 1997).
quote: the option that would allow the highest probability of success is generated first
limits: Review by advocates of the heuristics approach. States no dedicated independent replication list. Domain transfer claims are listed, not checked here.
agent_relevance: Take-the-first needs options generated in order of validity, which depends on learned experience. A base model that has not seen the task type has no such ordering.

source: Raab & Gigerenzer (2015), rival model comparison
finding: A rival theory exists. Long-term working memory (North et al. 2011) predicts that generating more options goes with better performance. Take-the-first predicts the reverse: more options, worse performance. This is a discriminating test between the two accounts.
numbers: Prediction signs only: positive (LTWM) vs negative (take-the-first) relation between number of options and performance.
limits: Result of the North et al. test is not reported in this review. Do not claim which side won.
agent_relevance: The open question for our scaffold: does adding candidates help or hurt? We should measure it per task type (best-of-N arm) rather than assume.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung effect, Cognition; summarised in Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (in press) Current Directions in Psychological Science
finding: Expert chess players who saw a familiar five-move smothered mate said they were looking for a shorter solution, but their eyes kept dwelling on the familiar solution. None of the Candidate Masters given the two-solution problem found the shorter mate in three. All found it when the familiar line was disabled.
numbers: Candidate Masters (3 SD above average): 0% found the shorter solution with the familiar one present, 100% when removed. The familiar first idea cut experts to the level of players about 3 SD weaker (IM matched Class A, Master matched Class B, Candidate Master matched Class C).
quote: reduced the problem solving performance of the experts to that of players about three standard deviations lower in skill
limits: Chess, one problem family per experiment, shortest-solution instruction. Table percentages in the text extract were garbled, so only the matching pairs and the 0% / 100% result are recorded.
agent_relevance: Strongest boundary on recognition: a strong first pattern blocks better options, and self-report ('I am searching') does not show it. The agent cannot trust its own claim that it explored alternatives (G2, G4).

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements, PLOS ONE
finding: Independent eye-tracking extension of Bilalic. Familiar move was suboptimal in problem 1: 8 of 17 experts and 8 of 17 novices still chose it. When the familiar move was a blunder (problems 2-4), all experts and most novices avoided it.
numbers: 34 players: 17 experts (CFC 1876-2580, mean 2223) and 17 novices. 3 minutes per problem; 4 test problems among 12 trials. Time to first fixation on the familiar region: experts 407 ms vs novices 719 ms (p<.01). Dwell duration 2395 vs 3440 ms (p<.05). The 16 who chose the familiar move kept fixating it.
limits: Small groups. Effect was much weaker when the familiar move failed visibly. Authors suggest immediate evidence of failure triggers search.
agent_relevance: Key boundary: a familiar first idea that visibly fails is dropped by everyone; one that merely looks fine is kept. This is the argument for G3: check against something the answer was not fitted to.

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013), expert vs novice detection
finding: Experts noticed the familiar-move region sooner (407 vs 719 ms) and had more separate dwells (27 vs 18), so recognition is faster in experts. Total dwell time and share of looking time did not differ significantly between groups.
numbers: Number of dwells: experts 27 vs novices 18 (p<.05). Total dwell time: no significant difference. Nine experts who found the optimal move gradually disengaged from the familiar region.
limits: Eye data on 34 players. Disengagement is correlational.
agent_relevance: Recognition speed rises with skill but does not by itself prevent lock-in. Disengagement happens only in some solvers, so the stop-and-switch rule needs an external trigger.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Naturalistic decision-making inspired prompts for LLM care-seeking advice, JMIR Biomedical Engineering 11:e88053 (press release read)
finding: Press release read in full. 10 ChatGPT models, including GPT-4o and GPT-5 series, were prompted with two NDM frames: recognition-primed (match symptoms to typical cases, simulate the outcome) and data-frame (build a frame, keep questioning it). Both raised overall accuracy. Self-care accuracy rose from 13.4% to nearly 30%. Emergency accuracy was kept. Non-reasoning models began identifying self-care cases.
numbers: Self-care: 13.4% default to nearly 30% with NDM prompts. N cases and overall accuracy not in the press release.
limits: Press release only; the article itself was blocked. Authors say it is best suited to controlled environments and real-user effect is untested.
agent_relevance: The only direct LLM test of RPD as a prompt that we found. Gain is in under-triage of mild cases, not in emergencies, so it is a calibration shift.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) JMIR Biomed Eng, figures from search summaries of the article and its preprint
finding: Search summaries give the design and numbers. 45 patient vignettes, three urgency levels, from a validated care-seeking framework. Published version: overall accuracy default 63.3%, RPD 67.6%, data-frame 66.7%. Self-care 13.4% to 29.8% (RPD) and 24.6% (data-frame). Preprint figures differed: default 64.7%, RPD 70.2%, data-frame 70.1%.
numbers: Published: 63.3% vs 67.6% vs 66.7% overall. Preprint: 64.7% vs 70.2% vs 70.1% (six models). 2 emergency and 30 nonemergency cases stayed high. The overall gain shrank by about 2.6 points between preprint and published version.
limits: JMIR pages were blocked, so these numbers are from search summaries and unverified. No CIs seen. Only 2 emergency cases limits any safety claim. Overall gain is about 3-4 points.
agent_relevance: Effect of an RPD-style prompt is small (about 3-4 points overall) and moved between versions. Treat as weak evidence, test before any S0 prompt change.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models (arXiv 2212.05206)
finding: GPT-3 family showed human-like intuitive errors on the Cognitive Reflection Test and semantic illusions, and more so than humans. ChatGPT models then shifted to correct answers, mostly via chain-of-thought written out. GPT-4 got 95% of CRT items right, humans 38%.
numbers: GPT-3-davinci-003 answered intuitively on 80% of CRT items and 72% of semantic illusions, vs humans 55% and 64%. ChatGPT-4: 95% CRT correct, 88% semantic illusions correct vs humans 38% and 26%. Chain-of-thought raised davinci-003 correct from 5% to 28%.
limits: Older models; trap-style items, not field decisions. Human comparison data were 41% CRT correct in original study n=3,428.
agent_relevance: Fast intuitive answers from a bare model are error-prone on trap tasks, and written reasoning fixes much of it. Supports gating S0 by task type, not using fast mode everywhere.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023), blocking chain of thought
finding: When ChatGPT was forced to answer without reasoning, ChatGPT-3.5 stayed about the same (no significant change in correct responses), while ChatGPT-4's correct responses fell only from 95% to 88% and intuitive errors rose from 0% to 10%. So a strong model carries trained intuition that works with little visible reasoning.
numbers: ChatGPT-4: correct 95% to 88% (p about .04), intuitive responses 0% to 10%. Chain-of-thought fraction fell from 97% to 0% (3.5) and 84% to 0% (GPT-4).
limits: CRT-style items only, which are memorized widely. The strong no-reasoning result may reflect training exposure, not general expertise.
agent_relevance: A model can have recognition-like skill on familiar item types, which is the S0 case. Familiarity may be contamination, so check on fresh items.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023), training examples build intuition
finding: Giving GPT-3 a few worked examples built a fast pattern response. Accuracy on some trap tasks climbed from near 0 to above 90% after two to seven examples, and to about 78% after 30 examples on the hardest set. This mirrors how experience builds recognition.
numbers: 2% to 92% after two examples (one task); 12% to 92% after seven examples; 0% to about 78% after 30 examples. Semantic illusions: 18% correct with 0 examples to over 64% with 10 or more.
limits: In-context examples of the same task type, so this tests pattern learning, not transfer. Only GPT-3.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples act as a cheap stand-in for domain experience. For S0, retrieved same-type solved examples may be the way to give the agent 'recognition'.

source: Chen et al. (2024/2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs, arXiv 2412.21187
finding: Reasoning models spend most of their tokens after they already have a correct first solution. In over 92% of cases the first round of solutions already contained the correct answer. Trimming redundant rounds cut tokens 48.6% with accuracy kept.
numbers: First round correct in over 92% of cases (QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1 on ASDIV and MATH500); first round under 60% of tokens (287 tokens, 38.7% of response, example on ASDIV). o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models on '2+3=?'. Token cut 48.6% with accuracy maintained.
limits: Easy sets (ASDIV, MATH500). On hard problems later rounds matter more. The extra solutions may be the model's version of checking.
agent_relevance: Machine analogue of take-the-first: the first answer is usually right on easy items. Supports a cheap S0 with early stopping when a check passes.

source: Zhu, Zheng & Jin (2025) FD-Bench: fine-grained evaluating the decision-making capability of LLM agents in dynamic scenarios, Cognitive Science Society
finding: Fire-evacuation benchmark (the NDM firefighting setting in miniature). 500 scenarios, 3,000 prompts, 8 LLMs. Performance drops by over 50% when the environment changes over time versus static. A hierarchical prompt (find dynamic elements, predict state, plan) improved success by up to 4.6%.
numbers: Over 50% drop dynamic vs static. Hierarchical guidance gain up to 4.6% (GPT-4 family). Rule induction for the complex rule (fire spread) was 21% or lower for every model in Table 3 (12-21% for the best GPT-4 rows). Table text was garbled, so per-model rows are not recorded.
limits: Grid world, not real firefighting. Table rows hard to read from the PDF. Gain is small.
agent_relevance: Time-changing situations are where recognition-from-text fails. The agent needs a state-tracking step, not only a first guess.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3, PNAS (arXiv 2206.14576)
finding: GPT-3 solves vignette decision tasks about as well as humans, beats humans on a multi-armed bandit task, but small changes to vignettes send it astray. It showed no directed exploration. On all three CRT items it gave the intuitive wrong answer. Even with a reworded CRT it kept saying the ball costs $0.10.
numbers: CRT: 3 of 3 items intuitive but incorrect. Bandit analysis over 13,000 problems from Peterson et al. (regret metric). Model-based RL signature shown (t(1814)=2.33, p=.01).
limits: Davinci, temperature 0, 2022. Newer models differ (see Hagendorff).
agent_relevance: Pattern recognition without exploration is a known weakness. Fits G1: doubt must be engineered by code since the model does not self-trigger it.

source: Grove, Zald, Lebow, Snitz & Nelson (2000) Clinical versus mechanical prediction: a meta-analysis, Psychological Assessment 12:19-30
finding: Meta-analysis of 136 studies: mechanical (formula) prediction was on average about 10% more accurate than clinical judgment, and was better or equal in most studies. Cited here from memory as the main boundary on expert intuition; not opened this session.
numbers: 136 studies; mechanical about 10% more accurate on average (from memory, verify). Clinicians' experience level did not close the gap (from memory, verify).
limits: Not opened. Prediction of outcomes in low-validity settings, not time-pressured action choice. Please verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Where outcomes are noisy, a counted rule beats judgment. Backs G5: code selects, the model does not judge.

source: Johnson & Raab (2003) and Raab & Johnson (2007), replication status
finding: The Raab & Gigerenzer review lists support for take-the-first in basketball (Hepler & Feltz 2011) and longitudinal development (Raab & Johnson 2007), but no preregistered or large independent replication is described. A web search for a dedicated replication of the 2003 handball result found none.
numbers: No replication N or effect size available.
limits: Absence in two sources is not proof of absence. Hepler & Feltz is cited only through the review.
agent_relevance: Take-the-first rests on a few sport studies by an advocate group. Count it as [S] single-tradition evidence.

source: Klein & Wright (2016), boundary: lab versus field
finding: Klein argues RPD could not have been found in the lab because it depends on 10-20 years of experience and lab studies use students on unfamiliar tasks. Lab critics reply that lack of control in NDM raises doubts about its results. The paper does not claim either side is correct.
numbers: 10-20 years of experience to build the pattern base.
limits: Explains why controlled tests are scarce, which is also why the evidence is thin.
agent_relevance: A model has no years of practice, only a large training set. Whether that counts as 10-20 years of recognition for a task type is untested and task dependent.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008), self-report mismatch
finding: All players who failed said they were looking for a shorter solution. Eye data showed they were still looking at the familiar solution and spent little time on squares needed for the shorter one. Players who got the one-solution version attended to key squares just before announcing the answer.
numbers: All expert players solved the 1-solution problem once the familiar solution was removed, including a separate group never exposed to the 2-solution problem (noted in footnote).
limits: Chess. Talk-aloud plus eye tracking, small groups of Candidate Masters.
agent_relevance: What the agent writes about its own search may not match what it did. Revision must be tied to real output (G2), and alternatives must be forced by code.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008), generality of lock-in
finding: The paper links this lock-in to experts elsewhere: doctors fixing on a first diagnosis, scientists and political experts ignoring negative evidence. The Luchins water-jar design is used as the base lay result, now reproduced with experts on complex problems.
numbers: Result held with a different problem set and the instruction 'find the best solution' rather than 'shortest' (stated, no figures).
limits: The medical and political links are citations in the text, not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Premature closure is the cost side of S0. Pair fast mode with a code-triggered check on the first candidate.

source: Klein, Calderwood & Clinton-Cirocco (1986) as summarised on Klein's own RPD page
finding: Klein's site says RPD explains how experienced commanders could act without generating and comparing a set of options. Core claim: people can use experience to generate a plausible option as the first one they consider. The page gives no numbers, no replications and no critiques.
numbers: None.
quote: people can use experience to generate a plausible option as the first one they consider
limits: Advocacy page. Useful only as the model's own statement of its claim.
agent_relevance: The claim is about option generation order, not about answer accuracy. Our S0 can borrow the order effect only if the model's first candidate is better than later ones.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026) Naturalistic decision-making
finding: Describes three RPD variants: act on the first course that comes to mind; use mental simulation to work out how the situation arose; evaluate each generated option and pick the best. States expertise is needed because simulation and evaluation depend on past events. NDM and controlled experiments are called complementary.
numbers: None. Born at a 1989 conference in Dayton, Ohio, leading to a 1993 book.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, no data. Secondary.
agent_relevance: The three variants map to: S0 quick pick, diagnose-first (reframe), and evaluate-then-pick. Only the simplest is the S0 case.

source: Search-result summary of Sheridan & Reingold (2013) and Bilalic et al. (2008) in a web search on Einstellung
finding: A second search summary says the companion Cognitive Psychology 2008 paper found the familiar solution induced Einstellung even in experts, and that Sheridan and Reingold found that when the familiar move was a blunder all experts and most novices avoided it. Agrees with the opened page, so the replication holds in direction.
numbers: As in b10.
limits: Duplicate of b10 from a secondary summary; kept to show the finding appeared in two forms.
agent_relevance: Same as b10.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009), moderator list from commentary
finding: Commentary summarising the paper says the key moderators are environment regularity and the amount and quality of feedback during practice. Subjective confidence is not a valid signal of accuracy. Not opened; from search snippet text only.
numbers: None.
limits: Secondary commentary only. The agent should not treat 'feels confident' as the S0 gate.
agent_relevance: Gate S0 by measured task-type accuracy, not by the model's stated confidence.
